title: Two pointers
summary: Two indices walking towards each other replace a slow nested loop.

cards.title: The slow way
cards.body: Find two numbers in a list that add up to a target. The obvious way: try every pair. With n numbers that's about n²/2 pairs, which is **O(n²)**.

cards.title: The clever way (sorted data)
cards.body:
Put one finger on the smallest number (`left`) and one on the biggest (`right`).

- Sum too small? Move `left` up to get a bigger number.
- Sum too big? Move `right` down to get a smaller one.

Each step rules out one number for good, so it takes at most n steps: **O(n)**.

cards.title: The code
cards.body: `std::pair<int, int>` returns two values at once. `{-1, -1}` means "no pair found".

cards.question: Array `[1, 3, 5, 8]`, target 9. `left` is at 1, `right` at 8. Sum = 9. What next?
cards.explain: 1 + 8 = 9 is exactly the target, so we're done.

cards.question: Why must the array be sorted for this trick?
choices: So that moving left up always makes the sum bigger (or equal)
cards.explain: The whole argument ("too small, so move left up") relies on values increasing from left to right.

cards.title: Build it: reverse in place
cards.body: Reversing an array is the simplest two-pointer algorithm: swap the ends, step inwards. Watch out for the empty vector.
